rationale: This archival historical political ecology study analyzes municipal drinking water governance in colonial Lima (1578-1700) using the Libros de Cabildos de Lima. Multiple governance mechanisms are empirically examined: (1) discretionary evaluation of connection petitions, route adjustments, and free license waivers awarded by Cabildo pipeline commissioners to council insiders, colonial elites, and religious orders (discretion_accommodation, the single most central mechanism reconstructed across Tables 4-6); (2) overlapping municipal public pipelines versus privately funded pipelines subject to public-fountain conditions (regulatory_model_ownership, Table 7); (3) weak compliance enforcement against illegal connections, excess water withdrawals above titled amounts, and convents' non-compliance with public-fountain mandates (enforcement_sanctions); and (4) connection license charges ranging from 100 to 500 pesos alongside selective exemptions (fees_tariffs_subsidies). Outcomes are co-equally focused on sociospatial disparities in household/institutional piped connections and network coverage (primary_connection, primary focal outcome mapped in Figures 3-4) and severe water shortages, service interruptions, and non-functioning public fountains in downstream and Indigenous neighborhoods (effective_access). The study design is an archival qualitative case study combining textual analysis of municipal council minutes with historical cartographic reconstruction.
